Data Entry Job Scams UK: Spot Fake Work-from-Home Offers

Scammers are using fake data entry job adverts to steal money and your personal details—here's how to protect yourself.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-07 · Updated 2026-07-30 · 7 min read

Quick answer: A data-entry job charging a starter fee, or a task platform demanding deposits to unlock commission or withdrawals, is a scam warning. Do not pay through an unverified recruiter link or private account, or route another person's money through your account. If you paid, contact your bank promptly. Report it to Report Fraud or Police Scotland on 101.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a data-entry job scam looks like

A data-entry job scam offers easy, well-paid work from home - typing, copy-pasting, form-filling, reviewing apps, or completing online tasks - to take your money, identity details, or bank access. An example of the style is: Earn £25/hour doing simple data entry from home. Pay a refundable £49 starter fee to receive your software and first batch.

Some versions are task scams. You are shown small early earnings, then told to deposit money to unlock higher commission, complete "combination tasks", or release withdrawals. Other versions are money-mule schemes dressed up as payment processing. This guide shows the warning signs, how to look for genuine work, and what to do if you have already paid.

Why these scams are convincing

The offer matches what many people want: flexible work, simple tasks, no commute, and quick income. The first steps can feel legitimate. Scammers may use real-sounding company names, fake dashboards, small early payouts, and recruiter messages on WhatsApp or Telegram.

The safest rule is practical: treat a supposed data-entry job that makes you pay to secure the role, unlock work, unlock withdrawals or receive wages as a scam warning. Separately, for most individual applicants, agencies cannot charge for finding work. The main sector exception covers specified entertainment and creative occupations, photographic or fashion modelling, and professional sport; separate rules can apply to some incorporated work-seekers and publication-only services. Data entry is not in that sector exception.

Our recruitment agency scam guide explains how the rules work, including why a separately offered service may only be charged for when access to work-finding is not conditional on buying it.

Signs a data-entry job is a scam

  • It asks for an upfront fee for software, training, a starter kit, registration, or onboarding.
  • It is a task, app-optimising, product-review, or "data boosting" job where you must deposit money to unlock commission or withdrawals.
  • It expects somebody else's money to pass through an account in your own name - bank, payment app or crypto wallet - whether that is described as processing, converting or forwarding it.
  • The pay is unusually high for very simple work and there is no real interview.
  • The recruiter moves you to WhatsApp, Telegram, or a personal email almost immediately.
  • It asks for bank details, passport images, National Insurance details, or other ID before a genuine offer.
  • The employer has no verifiable official website, careers page, address, or matching company record.

How the scam works

First, an advert or message offers easy, well-paid data entry from home. Second, you are moved off-platform and asked for a small starter fee, or you are placed in a fake task platform. Third, the platform shows supposed earnings. Fourth, you are told to deposit more money to continue, unlock commission, or withdraw. Fifth, the withdrawals never arrive or the account is locked behind more demands.

In the money-mule variant, the "job" wants a client's money routed through an account in your own name. Genuine payment-processing jobs exist, but they do not run other people's money through an employee's own bank account, payment account or crypto wallet, so stop at once if that is the ask. The National Crime Agency warns that money muling can lead to closed bank accounts and a criminal record, even where someone believed the work was genuine.

How to find data-entry work safely

Treat any pay-to-start offer as a red flag.

  • Do not pay a fee to begin a job, buy software, unlock tasks, or unlock withdrawals.
  • Be very wary of task platforms that require top-ups to earn commission.
  • Verify the employer independently through its official website, careers page, and a phone number you find yourself.
  • If it claims to be a UK limited company, compare the name, company number, address, and directors on Companies House. That is corroboration only: the register does not prove the vacancy or the recruiter is genuine, and filed information is not necessarily verified.
  • Apply through reputable job boards and keep messages on-platform where possible.
  • Never let a job route anyone else's money through an account you hold.

A criminal-record check is a different matter from paying to get work, and a genuine one can carry a published fee. Individuals can apply directly for a basic DBS check in England or Wales, a Level 1 disclosure in Scotland, or a basic AccessNI check in Northern Ireland; higher levels — including Level 2 and most PVG applications — are restricted to eligible roles and are started by an employer, organisation or registered body. Look the level, route and current fee up on that service before paying anyone.

Not sure a site is real? Our website-checking guide walks through it, and our work-from-home scam guide covers home-working scams more broadly.

If you paid or shared details

If you paid by card, contact your bank or card issuer using the number on your card. Tell them it was a scam and ask about disputing the payment or chargeback.

How to report a data-entry job scam (UK)

Report the listing or recruiter to the job board, social platform, or messaging platform you found it on. For an SMS, forward the message to 7726. For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; 7726 is not the in-app reporting route. Email phishing goes to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk.

Where money was lost, sensitive information was shared, or you were asked to move funds, the police report belongs with Report Fraud on reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 from England, Wales or Northern Ireland, and with Police Scotland on 101 from Scotland. Call your bank the same day if anything passed through your account.

Frequently asked questions

Is data-entry work from home ever genuine?

Yes, genuine data-entry and admin roles exist. The red flags are payment to start, unusually high pay for simple work, no real interview, task platforms that require deposits, and requests to receive and forward money.

I was asked to pay a starter or software fee - is that normal?

Do not pay a recruiter or private account to secure a job. In a genuine paid role you should not need to pay to unlock work, onboarding or wages, and an agency generally cannot charge an individual work-seeker for finding work — the main sector exception covers specified performing, creative, modelling and professional-sport occupations, which does not include data entry. A fee that can be real is a criminal-record check: check the level, route and current fee on DBS in England or Wales, Disclosure Scotland in Scotland, or AccessNI in Northern Ireland before paying anyone.

The job asks me to deposit money to unlock higher pay - what is that?

That is the task-scam pattern. You may see small early earnings, then be told to pay more to unlock commission or withdraw. Stop depositing and keep evidence.

I have already paid - can I get my money back?

Possibly. If you paid by card, ask your bank about disputing the payment. If you sent a bank transfer, an eligible domestic consumer payment by Faster Payments or retail CHAPS, made on or after 7 October 2024, may qualify for reimbursement under the APP rules: a maximum of £85,000, claimed inside 13 months, exclusions applying, and an excess of up to £100 that a firm cannot take from a consumer it assesses as vulnerable. None of it is a guaranteed refund.

How do I report a data-entry job scam?

Report the listing or recruiter to the platform. If you lost money, shared sensitive details, or were asked to move money, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Call your bank the same day if anything passed through your account.
